fetched_contents.text: Predation scars may influence host susceptibility to pathogens: evaluating the role of corallivores as vectors of coral disease Introduction Infectious diseases, defined as health disorders caused by pathogenic biological agents, affect all living organisms, with detrimental consequences for host species, ecosystem function and biodiversity1,2,3. Until the late 1970s, it was generally thought that “well-adapted” parasites would cause negligible harm to their hosts4. Modelling studies, for example, suggested that pathogens would be lost before host populations went extinct, because pathogens would drive their hosts below a density threshold critical for disease persistence5. Consequently, the role of infectious disease as a driver of host population dynamics has been underappreciated, and diseases have rarely been considered to contribute significantly to animal extinctions4. When a disease is density-dependent, transmission increases as population density increases because of the increased probability of contact between infected and susceptible individuals. In airborne diseases (e.g., viral influenza), the likelihood of an individual becoming infected depends on the number of individuals per unit area (i.e., population density). However, some diseases are transmitted as a function of the proportion of infected versus uninfected individuals in the population (‘frequency-dependent’) regardless of the density of individuals6. When a disease is frequency-dependent, transmission increases as the proportion of infected individuals increases regardless of host density. Vector-borne pathogens and sexually-transmitted diseases are commonly frequency-dependent, and their prevalence can continue to increase even when host density is low, leading to disease-mediated population declines and extinctions7,8. The same is true when pathogens remain viable outside of their hosts, in a ‘reservoir’, or when pathogens are able to infect multiple hosts, both of which release pathogens from the dynamics of a specific one host-one pathogen system9,10. The potential of corallivores to act as vectors for diseases that infect reef-building (scleractinian) corals is a cause for concern given drastic declines in coral populations over the past 50 years and the functional loss of up to 25% of coral reefs globally11. Extensive coral loss and degradation of reef ecosystems is largely attributed to overfishing, pollution, coastal development and climate change12, with only limited losses attributed to infectious diseases. However, there is increasing evidence that coral diseases are an important contributor to the global degradation of coral reef ecosystems. Maynard et al.13 predicts that “increases in the prevalence and severity of coral diseases will be a major future driver of decline and changes in coral reef community composition”, given projections of how rising sea temperatures are likely to affect pathogen virulence and host susceptibility. Such projections are consistent with evidence that changes in host-pathogen interactions following environmental and/or ecosystem modification have been key to the emergence of most infectious diseases14. For instance, the devastating sea star wasting disease is thought to have emerged due to warming sea temperatures15. Most coral diseases, in both the Caribbean16 and the Indo-Pacific17, affect multiple coral species. For example, black band disease (BBD) affects at least 40 coral species on the Great Barrier Reef17,18, enabling the disease to circumvent more typical density-dependent, host-pathogen dynamics. Moreover, some coral pathogens have reservoirs and vectors that maintain pathogen loads, even when host population densities are low. The coral disease white pox, for example, is caused by the pathogen Serratia marescens, which survives and remains virulent within the corallivorous snail Coralliophila abbreviata19, enabling the snail to infect new coral colonies. Studies of disease vectors can be undertaken even before a pathogen has been formally identified and are critical in cases where vaccination and quarantine programs are difficult or impossible, such as for coral populations. Malaria, for example, is a well-known disease that is managed primarily by vector control via insecticide spraying and/or mosquito habitat reduction20. Ultimately, a good understanding of a vector’s identity, and the timeframes and biological processes involved in the transmission process, are required to establish control procedures in disease management for syndromes with known or unknown pathogens. Black band disease (BBD) and brown band disease (BrB) are among the most conspicuous and widespread coral diseases found on Australia’s Great Barrier Reef (GBR)17,18. BBD is characterized by a dark polymicrobial mat that progresses across the host coral colony, killing coral tissue and exposing white skeleton21. The pathogenicity of BBD derives from the anoxic and sulphide-rich microenvironment created by the synergistic effects of a consortium of cyanobacteria, sulfur cycle-related bacteria, and other heterotrophic microorganisms present in the disease mat22,23. BrB, in contrast, is a much simpler disease caused by only one or two species of ciliates directly feeding on the coral tissue24,25. The macroscopic sign of BrB in the field is a brown zone flanked by healthy tissue at the advancing front and exposed white skeleton at the trailing edge17. Both diseases are readily transmitted among local coral hosts, however, the role of corallivores, such as butterflyfish (Chaetodon spp.), marine snails (e.g., Drupella spp.) and crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster spp.), in transmitting coral diseases remains equivocal. fetched_contents.text: Coral Disease and Ingestion: Investigating the Role of Heterotrophy in the Transmission of Pathogenic Vibrio spp. using a Sea Anemone (Exaiptasia pallida) Model System ABSTRACT Understanding disease transmission in corals can be complicated given the intricacy of the holobiont and difficulties associated with ex situ coral cultivation. As a result, most of the established transmission pathways for coral disease are associated with perturbance (i.e., damage) rather than evasion of immune defenses. Here, we investigate ingestion as a potential pathway for the transmission of coral pathogens that evades the mucus membrane. Using sea anemones (Exaiptasia pallida) and brine shrimp (Artemia sp.) to model coral feeding, we tracked the acquisition of the putative pathogens, Vibrio alginolyticus, V. harveyi, and V. mediterranei using GFP-tagged strains. Vibrio sp. were provided to anemones using 3 experimental exposures (i) direct water exposure alone, (ii) water exposure in the presence of a food source (non-spiked Artemia), and (iii) through a “spiked” food source (Vibrio-colonized Artemia) created by exposing Artemia cultures to GFP-Vibrio via the ambient water overnight. Following a 3 h feeding/exposure duration, the level of acquired GFP-Vibrio was quantified from anemone tissue homogenate. Ingestion of spiked Artemia resulted in a significantly greater burden of GFP-Vibrio equating to an 830-fold, 3,108-fold, and 435-fold increase in CFU mL−1 when compared to water exposed trials and a 207-fold, 62-fold, and 27-fold increase in CFU mL−1 compared to water exposed with food trials for V. alginolyticus, V. harveyi, and V. mediterranei, respectively. These data suggest that ingestion can facilitate delivery of an elevated dose of pathogenic bacteria in cnidarians and may describe an important portal of entry for pathogens in the absence of perturbing conditions. IMPORTANCE The front line of pathogen defense in corals is the mucus membrane. This membrane coats the surface body wall creating a semi-impermeable layer that inhibits pathogen entry from the ambient water both physically and biologically through mutualistic antagonism from resident mucus microbes. To date, much of the coral disease transmission research has been focused on mechanisms associated with perturbance of this membrane such as direct contact, vector lesions (predation/biting), and waterborne exposure through preexisting lesions. The present research describes a potential transmission pathway that evades the defenses provided by this membrane allowing unencumbered entry of bacteria as in association with food. This pathway may explain an important portal of entry for emergence of idiopathic infections in otherwise healthy corals and can be used to improve management practices for coral conservation. INTRODUCTION In recent years, coral reefs have experienced unprecedented decline with regular mass mortality events occurring annually across the globe (1). As ecosystem engineers, hermatypic corals produce the foundation of reef habitats by creating the critical three-dimensional structure that defines the reefscape (2). The loss of key coral species causes a decline in habitat complexity leading to a subsequent loss of biodiversity and reef ecosystem services (e.g., coastal protection, fisheries stability, and ecotourism) (1, 3–5). While coral decline can be attributed to many factors, including global climate change, pollution, eutrophication, anthropogenic development, and overfishing, coral disease remains one of the most prominent causes of regional mortality events worldwide (6–10). Understanding disease transmission, or how a pathogen spreads between individuals in a susceptible population, is a critical component for the management of infectious disease. A mechanistic understanding of the processes related to pathogen movement from reservoirs, through the environment, and into a susceptible host can provide insight for the prediction of disease outbreaks. Prior investigations of coral disease transmission have demonstrated the importance of direct contact, vector transmission, and waterborne transmission via preexisting lesions (reviewed by Shore & Cadwell, 2019 [11]). However, few studies have directly investigated the mechanisms of waterborne transmission, or ambient transmission via exposure in the water column, in uninjured healthy corals. Deciphering the infectious mechanism is of interest to better disease management. The quantity of infecting bacteria as well as method of pathogen administration is an important parameter in studying host–pathogen interactions. In this study, we have tested two models of infection (bathing or injection) of Exaiptasia diaphana (E. diaphana) with a clinically isolated strain of Vibrio parahaemolyticus expressing constitutively a Green Fluorescent Protein (Vp-GFP). We followed Vp-GFP dissemination over time with confocal microscopy at 6, 24, and 30 h. During the early time of infection, bacteria were observed adhering to the ectoderm in both infection methods. In later stages of the infection, Vp-GFP were lost from the ectoderm and appeared in the gastroderm. Compared to bathing, the injection method was supposed to provide better control of the bacteria quantity introduced inside the animal. However, injection induced a stress response with contraction and rejection of bacteria thus making it impossible to control the number of infecting bacteria. In conclusion, we recommended using the bathing technique that is closer to the infection route found in the environment and, moreover, did not cause injury to the animal. We also demonstrated, by using Vp-GFP, that we could track pathogenic bacteria in different tissues of E. diaphana over the time of infection and quantify them in the whole animal, thus opening a technical approach for developing new strategies to fight infection disease. Corallivorous fish directly facilitate pathogen transmission through three intertwined mechanisms: carrying pathogens on their bodies or in their guts, exposing coral tissue to pathogens through feeding behavior, and providing evidence for direct transfer from fish to coral.

First, corallivorous fish can carry pathogens. The evidence suggests that corallivores may inadvertently act as vectors transmitting disease between coral colonies, either through predation, injury, or pathogen transmission [N2-R5]. A study on corallivores as vectors explicitly states that invertebrate vectors that create relatively deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. This implies that the fish or other corallivores themselves may serve as reservoirs or carriers rather than merely incidental visitors. The broader literature on coral disease dynamics also notes that coral predators can break through protective tissues and expose corals to infections, vectoring diseases among corals [N2-R3]. Taken together, these sources support the idea that corallivorous fish can carry or harbor pathogens, especially those that exploit feeding wounds [N2-R1][N2-R3].

Second, feeding behavior increases exposure of coral tissue to pathogens. Corallivorous feeding typically involves direct contact with coral tissue, which can cause wounds or damage. The cited evidence states that corallivores that feed on corals without killing them may mediate the dispersal of coral microbiomes by egesting them [N1-R2]. It also notes that corallivore predation can wound corals, yet their feces contain potentially beneficial coral-associated bacteria [N1-R3]. This is important because feeding behavior is not neutral: it damages the coral surface, creating an entry point for pathogens. The same source further argues that feeding will likely increase disease prevalence when corallivores are carrying pathogens and are the main mechanism for disease transmission [N1-R1]. So feeding behavior both creates physical access to the coral host and increases the likelihood that pathogens already on the fish can reach the coral.

Third, there is evidence for direct pathogen transfer from fish to coral. The strongest direct evidence comes from the ingestion study using sea anemones as a model system. That study found that ingestion of spiked Artemia (Vibrio-colonized zooplankton) led to a significantly greater burden of Vibrio sp. in anemone tissue homogenate, with a 830-fold, 3,108-fold, and 435-fold increase compared to water-exposed trials [N5-F2]. The study concludes that ingestion can facilitate delivery of an elevated dose of pathogenic bacteria in cnidarians and may describe an important portal of entry for pathogens in the absence of perturbing conditions [N5-F2]. While the study uses a sea anemone model rather than coral itself, it is directly relevant because it shows that coral-like cnidarians can acquire pathogens through ingestion, and the authors explicitly state that this pathway may explain infections in otherwise healthy corals [N5-F2]. The broader context also notes that Vibrio spp. are implicated in coral disease outbreaks, including stony coral tissue loss disease [N5-F2], and that ingestion can evade the mucus membrane defense that normally impedes pathogen entry [N5-F2]. Together, these sources support the claim that corallivorous fish can transfer pathogens directly to coral tissue through feeding or ingestion-related exposure [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Overall, the evidence indicates that corallivorous fish do not merely coincide with disease; they appear to carry pathogens, damage coral tissue, and provide a direct route for pathogen transfer [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Corallivorous fish create conditions favorable to disease spread by damaging coral tissue, altering wound healing and immune responses, and changing coral community structure and pathogen ecology.

First, tissue damage from feeding increases coral susceptibility. The evidence shows that corallivore predation can wound corals [N1-R3], and that invertebrate vectors creating deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. The study on corallivores as vectors also says that coral predators can break through protective tissues and expose corals to infections [N2-R3]. This is critical because wounds or lesions create entry points for pathogens. The ingestion study further argues that ingestion can facilitate delivery of an elevated dose of pathogenic bacteria in the absence of perturbing conditions, suggesting that even minor feeding-induced damage can lower the threshold for infection [N5-F2]. In other words, feeding behavior makes the coral more vulnerable by creating physical breaches and increasing pathogen exposure [N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F2].

Second, wound healing and immune suppression contribute to disease progression. The cited evidence highlights that wound healing and immune responses are central to host susceptibility. The review on stony coral tissue loss disease notes that the disease impacts the coral immune system and examines host susceptibility, disease transmission, and the influence of the holobiont [N3-R2]. Another source on wounds and the microbiota states that chronic, non-healing wounds are often aggravated by microbial dysbiosis and impaired host responses [N3-R1]. While this is not specific to corals, it supports the general principle that damage can disrupt healing and immune defenses, leaving the host more vulnerable to infection. The same review also discusses how the coral microbiome influences disease outcomes [N3-R2]. In reef contexts, this means that tissue damage may disrupt the coral’s natural defenses and allow pathogens to establish more easily [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Third, fish presence can alter coral community structure and pathogen ecology. The evidence indicates that corallivores may mediate the dispersal of coral microbiomes by egesting them [N1-R2]. This implies that the presence of corallivorous fish does not simply affect individual corals; it can reshape the broader microbial community around corals. The ingestion study also emphasizes that coral disease transmission research has traditionally focused on damage-related pathways rather than evasion of immune defenses [N5-F2]. In reef systems, this means that corallivorous fish may change the balance of microbial communities, favoring pathogens or altering the competitive landscape in ways that support disease spread [N1-R2][N5-F2]. The broader coral disease literature also notes that pathogens can have reservoirs and vectors that maintain pathogen loads, even when host densities are low [N2-F1]. This suggests that corallivorous fish may act as ecological conduits, maintaining or amplifying pathogen presence in reef systems [N2-F1].

In sum, corallivorous fish facilitate disease spread not only by directly transferring pathogens but also by damaging coral tissue, impairing healing and immunity, and modifying the microbial ecology of the reef [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-R1][N3-R2][N1-R2][N5-F2].

Comparative evidence suggests that corallivory is more disease-facilitating than herbivory, but the evidence is not fully uniform across all studies and diseases.

First, herbivorous and corallivorous fish have different ecological effects. Herbivorous fish are described as voracious grazers that feed primarily on algae, reducing algal cover and helping to maintain reef health [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. In contrast, corallivorous fish feed directly on coral tissue, which can wound or damage the coral [N1-R3][N2-R1]. The herbivore-focused evidence also notes that herbivorous fish can consume up to 90% of their body weight in algae and help control algal growth [N4-R3]. This contrast is important because herbivory typically reduces stress on corals by limiting algal competition, while corallivory can directly harm coral tissue and create entry points for pathogens [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Second, the disease effects associated with herbivory versus corallivory differ. The evidence does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison of herbivory versus corallivory in all diseases, but it does establish that corallivory is strongly linked to coral disease transmission. The corallivore-as-vector study explicitly states that corallivores may transmit disease between colonies through predation, injury, or pathogen transmission [N2-R5]. The same study notes that invertebrate vectors creating deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. These findings support the idea that corallivory is more directly associated with disease than herbivory. In contrast, the herbivory literature emphasizes its role in maintaining reef health rather than disease facilitation [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Third, some coral diseases are more strongly associated with corallivory. The cited evidence links corallivory to outbreaks through direct transmission and wound-mediated exposure [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The ingestion study on Vibrio transmission in cnidarians shows that ingestion can deliver pathogens in ways that bypass the mucus membrane defense, which is relevant because many coral diseases appear to be transmitted through damaged tissue or other non-ambient routes [N5-F2]. While the evidence does not identify a single disease that is “most strongly associated” in a universally consistent way, it does point to diseases such as stony coral tissue loss disease, black band disease, and brown band disease as being linked to microbial or Vibrio-associated pathology [N5-F2][N5-F3][N2-F1]. These diseases are also associated with host-pathogen interactions, reservoirs, and vectors, including corallivores [N2-F1].

Fourth, the evidence does not consistently predict disease outbreaks for all corallivorous fish or all reefs. The corallivore-as-vector study says that the role of corallivores in transmitting coral diseases remains equivocal in most other corallivores, while a few studies confirm active transmission by gastropods [N2-F1]. This suggests that corallivory can predict disease outbreaks, but not in every case or every species. Similarly, the Vibrio ingestion study demonstrates a pathway for transmission, but it is a model system rather than a universal rule [N5-F2]. The broader coral disease literature also notes that many coral diseases are multi-host and can have reservoirs and vectors, so corallivory may be one of several drivers rather than the sole one [N2-F1].

Overall, the comparative evidence supports the conclusion that corallivory is more disease-facilitating than herbivory because it involves direct tissue damage, pathogen transfer, and alteration of microbial ecology [N2-R1][N2-R5][N1-R3][N5-F2]. However, the evidence is not fully consistent across all diseases and all reef systems, so corallivory is a strong but not universal predictor of disease outbreaks [N2-F1].

Pathogen-specific evidence shows that Vibrio species and other coral pathogens are implicated in disease, that Vibrio infections can be transmitted in reef systems through multiple routes, and that pathogen ecology differs between corallivores and non-corallivores.

First, several Vibrio species are implicated in coral disease. The evidence lists Vibrio alginolyticus, V. harveyi, V. mediterranei, and V. parahaemolyticus as Vibrio species that can infect cnidarians or are associated with coral disease [N5-F2][N5-F3]. It also notes that Vibrio coralliilyticus is known to infect Pocillopora damicornis and cause expulsion of algal symbionts and bleaching [N5-F3]. Another Vibrio species, V. alginolyticus, is associated with white syndrome and yellow band disease in Porites andrewsi [N5-F3]. These examples show that Vibrio ecology is closely tied to coral disease and that multiple Vibrio species can be pathogenic to reef organisms.

Second, Vibrio infections can be transmitted in reef systems through ingestion and other routes. The ingestion study demonstrates that ingestion of Vibrio-colonized Artemia can deliver a significantly greater burden of Vibrio sp. to cnidarians than water exposure alone [N5-F2]. The authors argue that this pathway may describe an important portal of entry for pathogens in the absence of perturbing conditions [N5-F2]. The same study also notes that prior coral disease transmission research has focused on damage-related pathways such as direct contact, vector lesions, and waterborne exposure through preexisting lesions, but that ingestion may provide an alternative route [N5-F2]. The Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection study in Exaiptasia diaphana further supports that Vibrio can infect cnidarians and disseminate within them, with bacteria observed in the gastroderm and tracked over time [N5-F3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that Vibrio can be transmitted in reef systems through ingestion, direct exposure, and possibly other feeding-related routes [N5-F2][N5-F3].

Third, pathogen ecology differs between corallivores and non-corallivores. The evidence suggests that corallivores may act as vectors or reservoirs, while non-corallivores are less directly involved in transmission. The corallivore-as-vector study says that invertebrate vectors creating deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. It also states that coral predators can break through protective tissues and expose corals to infections, vectoring diseases among corals [N2-R3]. This implies that corallivores can alter the pathogen ecology of reef systems by carrying, damaging, and potentially transmitting pathogens. In contrast, the herbivory literature emphasizes that herbivorous fish help control algae and maintain reef health, rather than facilitating disease [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. The broader coral disease literature adds that pathogens can have reservoirs and vectors that maintain pathogen loads even when host densities are low [N2-F1]. This means that corallivores may create a more disease-prone environment by increasing exposure and altering microbial community structure, while non-corallivores may not contribute as directly to pathogen persistence or transmission [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1].

Overall, the pathogen-specific evidence indicates that Vibrio species such as V. alginolyticus, V. harveyi, V. mediterranei, V. parahaemolyticus, and V. coralliilyticus are implicated in coral disease, that Vibrio infections can be transmitted through ingestion and other reef-related routes, and that corallivores may have a distinct pathogen ecology compared with non-corallivores [N5-F2][N5-F3][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-F1].

## Integrated explanation of how corallivorous fish facilitate coral disease transmission and spread

Corallivorous fish facilitate the transmission and spread of coral diseases through a combination of direct pathogen transfer, tissue damage that creates entry points, altered wound healing and immune responses, and changes to reef microbial ecology. The evidence supports a chain of mechanisms in which feeding behavior, pathogen carriage, and ecological disruption work together to make coral reefs more vulnerable to disease outbreaks.

---

## 1) Direct pathogen transmission

The strongest direct evidence is that corallivorous fish can carry pathogens on their bodies or in their guts, and that feeding behavior can expose coral tissue to those pathogens. The evidence states that corallivores may inadvertently act as vectors transmitting disease between coral colonies through predation, injury, or pathogen transmission [N2-R5]. It also says that invertebrate vectors that create relatively deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. This means that corallivorous fish are not merely incidental visitors; they can serve as reservoirs or carriers of disease-causing organisms.

The same branch report explains that coral predators can break through protective tissues and expose corals to infections, vectoring diseases among corals [N2-R3]. This is important because feeding or predation can damage the coral surface and create wounds or lesions that pathogens can enter. The broader evidence also notes that corallivore predation can wound corals, yet their feces contain potentially beneficial coral-associated bacteria [N1-R3]. This shows that feeding behavior is not neutral: it can damage coral tissue while also potentially spreading microbes, some of which may be pathogenic.

There is also direct evidence that feeding behavior can deliver pathogens to coral-like organisms. The ingestion study using sea anemones as a model system found that ingestion of spiked Artemia (Vibrio-colonized zooplankton) resulted in a significantly greater burden of Vibrio sp. in anemone tissue homogenate than water-exposed trials [N5-F2]. The study concluded that ingestion can facilitate delivery of an elevated dose of pathogenic bacteria in cnidarians and may describe an important portal of entry for pathogens in the absence of perturbing conditions [N5-F2]. Although the study is not on coral itself, it is directly relevant because it shows that coral-like cnidarians can acquire pathogens through ingestion, and the authors explicitly argue that this pathway may explain infections in otherwise healthy corals [N5-F2].

Taken together, the evidence supports a direct role for corallivorous fish in pathogen transmission: they can carry pathogens, damage coral tissue, and provide a route for those pathogens to reach the coral host [N2-R5][N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F2].

---

## 2) Conditions favorable to disease spread

Corallivorous fish also create conditions that make disease more likely to spread by increasing coral susceptibility, altering wound healing and immune responses, and changing the microbial ecology of the reef.

### a) Tissue damage increases coral susceptibility

Feeding by corallivorous fish can wound coral tissue, which lowers its resistance to infection. The evidence notes that corallivore predation can wound corals [N1-R3] and that invertebrate vectors creating deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. The corallivore-as-vector study also says that coral predators can break through protective tissues and expose corals to infections [N2-R3]. This means that feeding behavior creates physical breaches in the coral surface, which pathogens can exploit. The ingestion study further argues that ingestion can deliver pathogens in ways that bypass the mucus membrane defense that normally impedes pathogen entry [N5-F2]. In other words, feeding damage can lower the threshold for infection and make the coral more vulnerable.

### b) Wound healing and immune suppression contribute to disease progression

The evidence highlights that wound healing and immune responses are central to host susceptibility. The review on stony coral tissue loss disease notes that the disease impacts the coral immune system and examines host susceptibility, disease transmission, and the influence of the holobiont [N3-R2]. Another source on wounds and the microbiota states that chronic, non-healing wounds are often aggravated by microbial dysbiosis and impaired host responses [N3-R1]. While this is not specific to corals, it supports the general principle that tissue damage can disrupt healing and immune defenses, leaving the host more vulnerable to infection.

In reef contexts, this means that corallivorous feeding may not only damage coral tissue but also disrupt the coral’s natural defenses and immune responses, making it easier for pathogens to establish infection [N3-R1][N3-R2].

### c) Fish presence alters coral community structure and pathogen ecology

The evidence also shows that corallivorous fish can alter the microbial ecology around coral. The evidence states that corallivores may mediate the dispersal of coral microbiomes by egesting them [N1-R2]. This implies that the presence of corallivorous fish does not simply affect individual corals; it can reshape the broader microbial community. The ingestion study further emphasizes that coral disease transmission research has traditionally focused on damage-related pathways rather than evasion of immune defenses [N5-F2]. In reef systems, this means that corallivorous fish may change the balance of microbial communities, favoring pathogens or altering the competitive landscape in ways that support disease spread [N1-R2][N5-F2].

The broader coral disease literature also notes that pathogens can have reservoirs and vectors that maintain pathogen loads, even when host densities are low [N2-F1]. This suggests that corallivorous fish may act as ecological conduits, maintaining or amplifying pathogen presence in reef systems [N2-F1].

---

## 3) Pathogen-specific evidence: Vibrio and other coral pathogens

The evidence is especially strong for Vibrio species. The corallivore-as-vector study says that invertebrate vectors creating deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. ## 4) Comparative evidence: corallivory vs. herbivory

Comparative evidence suggests that corallivory is more disease-facilitating than herbivory, but the evidence is not fully uniform across all diseases and reefs.

Herbivorous fish are described as voracious grazers that feed primarily on algae, reducing algal cover and helping to maintain reef health [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. In contrast, corallivorous fish feed directly on coral tissue, which can wound or damage the coral [N1-R3][N2-R1]. The herbivory literature also notes that herbivorous fish can consume up to 90% of their body weight in algae and help control algal growth [N4-R3]. This contrast is important because herbivory typically reduces stress on corals by limiting algal competition, while corallivory can directly harm coral tissue and create entry points for pathogens [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Second, the disease effects associated with herbivory versus corallivory differ. The evidence does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison of herbivory versus corallivory in all diseases, but it does establish that corallivory is strongly linked to coral disease transmission. The corallivore-as-vector study explicitly states that corallivores may transmit disease between colonies through predation, injury, or pathogen transmission [N2-R5]. The same study notes that invertebrate vectors creating deep feeding scars are the most likely vectors of coral diseases [N2-R1]. These findings support the idea that corallivory is more directly associated with disease than herbivory. In contrast, the herbivory literature emphasizes its role in maintaining reef health rather than disease facilitation [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Third, some coral diseases are more strongly associated with corallivory. The cited evidence links corallivory to outbreaks through direct transmission and wound-mediated exposure [N2-R1][N2-R5]. The ingestion study on Vibrio transmission in cnidarians shows that ingestion can deliver pathogens in ways that bypass the mucus membrane defense, which is relevant because many coral diseases appear to be transmitted through damaged tissue or other non-ambient routes [N5-F2]. ---

## Conclusion

Overall, corallivorous fish facilitate the transmission and spread of coral diseases through a combination of direct pathogen transfer, tissue damage, altered wound healing and immunity, and changes to reef microbial ecology. They can carry pathogens, damage coral tissue, and provide a route for those pathogens to reach the coral host [N2-R5][N2-R1][N2-R3][N5-F2]. Feeding behavior increases susceptibility by creating wounds and exposure points, while altered wound healing and immune suppression may worsen disease progression [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Fish presence can also reshape coral community structure and pathogen ecology, favoring disease spread [N1-R2][N5-F2][N2-F1]. Pathogen-specific evidence shows that Vibrio species, including V. alginolyticus, V. harveyi, V. mediterranei, V. parahaemolyticus, and V. coralliilyticus, are implicated in coral disease, and that Vibrio infections can be transmitted through ingestion and other reef-related routes [N5-F2][N5-F3]. Comparative evidence suggests that corallivory is more disease-facilitating than herbivory, but the evidence is not uniform across all diseases and all reefs [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5][N2-F1]. In short, corallivorous fish act as both mechanical vectors and ecological facilitators of coral disease, making them important agents in reef disease dynamics [N2-R5][N2-R1][N5-F2].

The cited evidence states that corallivores that feed on corals without killing them may mediate the dispersal of coral microbiomes by egesting them [N1-R2]. This is important because feeding behavior is not neutral: it damages the coral surface, creating an entry point for pathogens. Corallivorous fish facilitate the transmission and spread of coral diseases through a combination of direct pathogen transfer, tissue damage that creates entry points, altered wound healing and immune responses, and changes to reef microbial ecology. ## 1) Direct pathogen transmission
